title: When you can't stand
hookLine: you pray sitting, lying, or by signs; the prayer bends to the body

lines: A ROW OF CHAIRS AT THE BACK.
cards: Walk into almost any mosque today and look along the back wall. There's a row of plastic chairs. An older man sits in one, and when the line bows, he leans forward from his seat.
When they go down to the floor, he leans a little further. Nobody looks twice. Across town, in a hospital bed, a woman who can't sit up at all moves her eyes and her lips through the same prayer.
For ten days now, this path has followed the body as it stands, bows and falls to the ground. So what happens when the body can't?

teach.b: A short hadith in Bukhari answers it. A companion named Imran ibn Husayn had a painful illness and asked the Prophet ﷺ how to pray. The answer was three lines.
Pray standing. If you can't, then sitting. If you can't, then on your side.

teach.h: BY SIGNS, OR WITH THE EYES.
teach.b: Scholars filled in the rest: if you can't bow or prostrate, you make the movements with signs, leaning or nodding, a little lower for the prostration than for the bow.
If you can't move at all, with your eyes, or in your heart. The prayer keeps going; it just gets smaller to fit. The Prophet himself did this.
When he fell from a horse and hurt his side, he prayed sitting, and in his last illness he prayed sitting, too.
Underneath is one of the best-known lines in the Qur'an, from the end of Surah al-Baqarah, in Pickthall's words: "Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope." Scope: what it can hold.

The prayer is an obligation, and one that bends to the person. So is the washing, which becomes tayammum without water, and the four rak'ahs that become two on a journey, and, as you'll see, the fast.
The prayer isn't only for the strong, the flexible, the young. The man in the plastic chair isn't praying a lesser prayer. In the tradition, he's doing exactly what's asked of him.

how: Muslims who can't stand pray sitting, often on a chair, leaning forward for the bow and a little further for the prostration; those who can't sit pray lying on their side or back, using signs with the head or eyes.

o: washing the whole body after a long trip
a quick rinse of the hands before eating
the dry washing used when there's no water

games.q: what's inside the ladder — tap the pairs.
p: asked how to pray when ill
a little lower than the bow

s: someone who prays in a chair is praying a lesser prayer
in the tradition, they're doing exactly what's asked of them; the Prophet ﷺ himself prayed sitting when hurt.
the Qur'an says Allah tasks no soul beyond its scope
someone who can't stand is excused from the prayer entirely
the prayer continues: sitting, on the side, or by signs.

games.q: you're Imran ibn Husayn, ill and in pain, and you ask the Prophet ﷺ how to pray. what does he say?
o: standing; if you can't, sitting; if you can't, on your side
games.why: three lines in Bukhari: pray standing, if you can't then sitting, if you can't then on your side. the prayer bends to the body.

practice: Stay in your chair: raise your hands for the opening, rest them, and sit tall for the standing.

Lean forward from the hips for the bow, come back up, then lean a little further for each prostration, lower than the bow, sitting back between, slowly, the way someone moves when this is what the body allows.
If you pray, you can say the words as you go.

wordCard.voice: Tayammum, the dry washing used when there's no water, one more way the prayer bends to the body: sitting if you can't stand, on your side if you can't sit, by signs if you can't move.

carryVoice: Your line: the prayer fits you. It steps down to meet the body it has. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1117 (Imran ibn Husayn: standing, sitting, on your side)
Sahih al-Bukhari 378 and 688 (the Prophet praying sitting after his fall, and in his last illness)
